facts.fact: The US-Mozambique health MOU signed on 15 December 2025 states that the Integrated Electronic Medical Record System (SIS-RME) is owned and operated by the Government of Mozambique, and that data systems the US funds are to be fully led and owned by the Government with US technical assistance and workplan oversight (sections 2.5.1 and 2.5.2).

The MOU states the US Government plans to fund SIS-RME's software development, equipment, the transition of SESP's functions, data-capture improvements and integration into the health data exchange, within US$83,072,079 of data-systems funding over 2026-2030 (US$16,666,385 in 2026); Mozambique commits only to pay ongoing licensing, cloud and hardware costs the US does not pay, and no Mozambican amount is given.

The MOU, running from 1 April 2026 to 31 December 2030, names SIS-RME as the core product of the national digital health platform, with a yearly data-systems funding plan and a Data Systems Roadmap holding its development and deployment detail; a minimum viable version is targeted for September 2026 with modules for registration, consultation, maternal and child health, and HIV and TB services for inpatients and outpatients.

On 15 December 2025 Mozambique and the United States signed an MOU committing Mozambique to implement SIS-RME, with a minimum viable version targeted for release in September 2026, the US-built patient tracking system SESP to pass to Mozambican management by 20 June 2026 and be retired once migrated into SIS-RME, and a scannable data-capture solution for low-burden health facilities by the end of June 2027.

slug: 2021-08-04 Health information systems in developing countries case of African countries

facts.fact: A literature review carried out February-July 2019 (Koumamba et al., citing a 2013 African Health Initiative paper) states that Mozambique, like Ghana, adapted the DHIS software from its standardised tools in order to record aggregated data at the facility, district and regional levels; it gives no count of facilities entering data.

The same review states that Mozambique was one of the countries that received support from the International Health Partnership and used the DHIS software to implement its health information system, and that most such projects were supported by external donors; review carried out February-July 2019.

The review found that 11 of the 12 African countries studied, Mozambique among them and Malawi the only exception, had no national health information strategy, only strategies implemented under a specific project and aligned with donors; review carried out February-July 2019.

facts.fact: A 2019 assessment by the University of Oslo, Eduardo Mondlane University and the Ministry of Health (Collinson et al.), covering 14 districts and 8 health units in six provinces, found that facilities' monthly data reached the district health office (SDSMAS) on paper forms, were validated there on paper or in Excel, and only then were entered into SISMA, in most districts visited by the district statistical officers, with entry shared with programme officers in Cuamba and delegated to nurses in Bilene and Cumbane.

Collinson et al. report from their 2019 assessment that SISMA is the national health information system platform, that registering users and configuring services and health facilities are done centrally at the Ministry of Health, that support passes from district and provincial statisticians to technical teams at the Ministry, and that an external team linked to the platform's owner gives further support under agreement with the Ministry.

Collinson et al. report that at the health facilities visited in 2019 (8 health units in five provinces) daily registries were collected in paper books and charts, beside tablets supplied by particular programmes to collect specific data; the paper names no patient record system.
